W4. Functions and Their Graphs, Elementary Functions and Properties

Author

Zakhar Podyakov

Published

September 18, 2025

Quiz | Flashcards

1. Summary

1.1 Core Concepts of Functions

A function is a rule that assigns a single, unique output to every input. The set of all permissible inputs is called the domain, and the set of all resulting outputs is the range. If a function f takes an input x to produce an output y, we write \(y = f(x)\).

  • Implicit Domain: When a function is defined by a formula without a specified domain, the domain is assumed to be the largest set of real numbers for which the formula gives real-valued outputs. For example, for \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x-2}\), the domain is all real numbers except \(x=2\).
  • Graph of a Function: The graph is a visual representation consisting of all points \((x, f(x))\) on the Cartesian plane. The value \(f(x)\) represents the height of the graph at point \(x\). The formal definition of the graph is the set \(\{(x, f(x)) | x \in D\}\), where \(D\) is the domain.
1.2 Special Step Functions: Floor and Ceiling
  • Floor Function (Greatest Integer Function): Denoted \(\lfloor x \rfloor\), this function rounds a number down to the greatest integer less than or equal to \(x\). For example, \(\lfloor 3.7 \rfloor = 3\) and \(\lfloor -2.1 \rfloor = -3\).
  • Ceiling Function (Least Integer Function): Denoted \(\lceil x \rceil\), this function rounds a number up to the smallest integer greater than or equal to \(x\). For example, \(\lceil 3.7 \rceil = 4\) and \(\lceil -2.1 \rceil = -2\).
1.3 Function Behavior: Monotonicity

A function is monotone on an interval if it consistently increases or decreases.

  • Increasing: \(f(x_1) \le f(x_2)\) whenever \(x_1 < x_2\).
  • Strictly Increasing: \(f(x_1) < f(x_2)\) whenever \(x_1 < x_2\).
  • Decreasing: \(f(x_1) \ge f(x_2)\) whenever \(x_1 < x_2\).
  • Strictly Decreasing: \(f(x_1) > f(x_2)\) whenever \(x_1 < x_2\).

A function that is strictly monotone (either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing) on its domain is guaranteed to be one-to-one.

1.4 Combining Functions

Functions can be combined arithmetically or through composition. For arithmetic combinations, the domain is the intersection of the individual domains.

  • Arithmetic Operations: \((f+g)(x) = f(x)+g(x)\); \((f-g)(x) = f(x)-g(x)\); \((fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)\); and \((f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x)\), with the added domain restriction that \(g(x) \neq 0\).
  • Composition: The composition \((f \circ g)(x)\) is defined as \(f(g(x))\). The input \(x\) must be in the domain of \(g\), and the output \(g(x)\) must be in the domain of \(f\). The order of composition is critical, as \((f \circ g)(x)\) is generally not equal to \((g \circ f)(x)\).
1.5 Inverse Functions
  • One-to-One Function: A function is one-to-one if no two distinct inputs produce the same output. This can be verified visually with the horizontal line test—if no horizontal line intersects the graph more than once, the function is one-to-one.
  • Inverse Function: If a function \(f\) is one-to-one, it has an inverse function, denoted \(f^{-1}\), that “reverses” its action. If \(f(a) = b\), then \(f^{-1}(b) = a\). The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\). The graph of \(f^{-1}\) is a reflection of the graph of \(f\) across the line \(y=x\).
1.6 Function Symmetry: Even and Odd Functions

For a function to be even or odd, its domain must be symmetric about the origin (if \(x\) is in the domain, \(-x\) must also be).

  • Even Function: \(f\) is even if \(f(-x) = f(x)\). Its graph is symmetric with respect to the y-axis (e.g., \(f(x) = x^2\), \(f(x) = \cos x\)).
  • Odd Function: \(f\) is odd if \(f(-x) = -f(x)\). Its graph is symmetric with respect to the origin (e.g., \(f(x) = x^3\), \(f(x) = \sin x\)).

Any function with a symmetric domain can be uniquely decomposed into the sum of an even and an odd function:

  • Even Part: \(f_{\text{even}}(x) = \frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2}\)
  • Odd Part: \(f_{\text{odd}}(x) = \frac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2}\)
1.7 Elementary Functions
1.7.1 Power, Polynomial, and Rational Functions
  • Power Function: A function of the form \(f(x) = x^a\), where \(a\) is a real number. This includes integer powers (\(x^2\)), roots (\(x^{1/2} = \sqrt{x}\)), and reciprocals (\(x^{-1} = 1/x\)).
  • Polynomial Function: A sum of power functions with non-negative integer exponents: \(p(x) = a_n x^n + \dots + a_1 x + a_0\). The highest exponent \(n\) is the degree of the polynomial.
  • Rational Function: A ratio of two polynomials, \(f(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\). Its domain excludes any values of \(x\) for which \(q(x)=0\).
1.7.2 Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
  • Exponential Function: \(f(x) = a^x\), where the base \(a > 0\) and \(a \neq 1\). Its domain is all real numbers, and its range is \((0, \infty)\).
  • Logarithmic Function: \(f(x) = \log_a(x)\), the inverse of the exponential function. The expression \(\log_a(x)\) gives the exponent to which the base \(a\) must be raised to obtain \(x\). Its domain is \((0, \infty)\), and its range is all real numbers.
1.7.3 Trigonometric Functions and Their Inverses

Trigonometric functions relate an angle \(\theta\) to the coordinates \((x, y)\) of a point on a circle of radius \(r\). They are periodic, meaning their values repeat.

  • Definitions: \(\sin \theta = y/r\), \(\cos \theta = x/r\), \(\tan \theta = y/x\), etc.
  • Periodicity: The period of \(\sin x, \cos x, \sec x, \csc x\) is \(2\pi\). The period of \(\tan x\) and \(\cot x\) is \(\pi\).
  • Inverse Trigonometric Functions: Because they are not one-to-one, we must restrict the domain of trigonometric functions to create their inverses (e.g., \(\arcsin x\), \(\arccos x\)). For example, \(\arcsin x\) is defined for inputs in \([-1, 1]\) and produces an angle in \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\).
1.7.4 Hyperbolic Functions and Their Inverses

Hyperbolic functions are combinations of exponential functions and are analogous to trigonometric functions.

  • Definitions: \(\sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}\) and \(\cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}\). The other four are defined similarly to their trigonometric counterparts (e.g., \(\tanh x = \sinh x / \cosh x\)).
  • Inverse Hyperbolic Functions: These are the inverses of the hyperbolic functions (with domain restrictions where needed, like for \(\cosh x\)). They can be expressed using natural logarithms. For instance, \(\text{arsinh}(x) = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2+1})\).

2. Definitions

  • Function: A rule assigning each input from a domain to exactly one output.
  • Domain: The set of all possible input values for a function.
  • Range: The set of all possible output values of a function.
  • One-to-One Function: A function where each output corresponds to a unique input.
  • Inverse Function (\(f^{-1}\)): A function that reverses the mapping of a one-to-one function.
  • Even Function: A function satisfying \(f(-x) = f(x)\), symmetric about the y-axis.
  • Odd Function: A function satisfying \(f(-x) = -f(x)\), symmetric about the origin.
  • Periodic Function: A function that repeats its values at regular intervals (the period).
  • Polynomial: A function expressed as a sum of non-negative integer powers of a variable.
  • Degree of a Polynomial: The highest exponent of the variable in a polynomial.
  • Rational Function: A function that is the ratio of two polynomials.
  • Exponential Function: A function of the form \(f(x) = a^x\) where \(a\) is a positive constant.
  • Logarithmic Function: The inverse of an exponential function, \(f(x) = \log_a(x)\).
  • Hyperbolic Functions: Functions defined as combinations of \(e^x\) and \(e^{-x}\), such as \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\).
  • Composition of Functions: An operation \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\) where one function is applied to the result of another.

3. Formulas

  • Even Part of a Function: \[f_{\text{even}}(x) = \frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2}\]
  • Odd Part of a Function: \[f_{\text{odd}}(x) = \frac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2}\]
  • Function Composition: \[(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\]
  • Finding an Inverse Function: \(y=f(x) \implies x=f^{-1}(y)\)
  • Pythagorean Identity: \[\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\]
  • Inverse Trigonometric Identity: \[\arcsin(x) + \arccos(x) = \frac{\pi}{2}\]
  • Inverse Sine as an Odd Function: \[\arcsin(-x) = -\arcsin(x)\]
  • Inverse Reciprocal Identity: \[\arcsin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = \text{arccsc}(x)\]
  • Hyperbolic Sine Definition: \[\sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}\]
  • Hyperbolic Cosine Definition: \[\cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}\]
  • Hyperbolic Identity: \[\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1\]
  • Hyperbolic-Inverse Trig Identities:
    • \(\sinh(\text{arccosh } x) = \sqrt{x^2 - 1}\)
    • \(\sinh(\text{arctanh } x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\)
    • \(\cosh(\text{arcsinh } x) = \sqrt{1+x^2}\)
    • \(\cosh(\text{arctanh } x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\)
    • \(\tanh(\text{arcsinh } x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\)
    • \(\tanh(\text{arccosh } x) = \frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x}\)
  • Logarithmic Form of arsinh: \[\text{arsinh}(x) = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2+1})\]
  • Logarithmic Form of arcosh: \[\text{arcosh}(x) = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2-1})\]
  • Logarithmic Form of artanh: \[\text{artanh}(x) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\]
  • Logarithmic Form of arcsch: \[\text{arcsch}(x) = \ln\left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|}\right)\]
  • Logarithmic Form of arsech: \[\text{arsech}(x) = \ln\left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}\right)\]
  • Logarithmic Form of arcoth: \[\text{arcoth}(x) = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right)\]
  • Sum of Cubes: \[1^3 + 2^3 + \dots + n^3 = \frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}\]
  • Complex Number Modulus: For \(z = a+ib\), \[|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\]
  • Complex Number Trigonometric Form: \[z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\]
  • Complex Number Exponential Form: \[z = re^{i\theta}\]
  • Complex Number Division: \[\frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{z_1 \bar{z_2}}{|z_2|^2}\]

4. Examples

4.1. Prove Hyperbolic and Inverse Function Identities (Chapter 2, Task 1)

Prove the following identities involving hyperbolic and inverse hyperbolic/trigonometric functions.

  1. \(\sinh(\text{arccosh } x) = \sqrt{x^2 - 1}; \quad |x| \ge 1\)
  2. \(\sinh(\text{arctanh } x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}; \quad -1 < x < 1\)
  3. \(\cosh(\text{arcsinh } x) = \sqrt{1+x^2}\)
  4. \(\cosh(\text{arctanh } x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}; \quad -1 < x < 1\)
  5. \(\tanh(\text{arcsinh } x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\)
  6. \(\tanh(\text{arccosh } x) = \frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x}; \quad |x| \ge 1\)
Click to see the solution

The proofs for (1), (3), and (6) are shown in other tasks. The others follow a similar pattern. Let’s prove (2) as an example.

  1. Let \(y = \text{arctanh } x\). By definition, this means \(x = \tanh y\).
  2. Use hyperbolic identities. We know the identity \(\text{sech}^2 y = 1 - \tanh^2 y\). Since \(\cosh y = \frac{1}{\text{sech } y}\), we have \(\cosh^2 y = \frac{1}{1 - \tanh^2 y} = \frac{1}{1-x^2}\).
  3. Find \(\cosh y\). Since the range of arctanh is all real numbers, but \(\cosh y\) is always positive, we take the positive root: \(\cosh y = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\).
  4. Find \(\sinh y\). We know \(\tanh y = \frac{\sinh y}{\cosh y}\), so \(\sinh y = \tanh y \cosh y\).
  5. Substitute: \(\sinh y = x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\).
  6. Conclusion: Since \(y = \text{arctanh } x\), we have shown \(\sinh(\text{arctanh } x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\).
4.2. Floor and Ceiling Functions (Chapter 2, Example)

Explain the floor function (\(\lfloor x \rfloor\)) and the ceiling function (\(\lceil x \rceil\)) and provide examples for the inputs 2.4, 1.9, 0, -1.2, 2, 0.2, and -0.3.

Click to see the solution
  1. Floor Function \(\lfloor x \rfloor\):
    • Definition: The floor function, also called the greatest integer function, gives the greatest integer that is less than or equal to \(x\).
    • Examples:
      • \(\lfloor 2.4 \rfloor = 2\)
      • \(\lfloor 1.9 \rfloor = 1\)
      • \(\lfloor 0 \rfloor = 0\)
      • \(\lfloor -1.2 \rfloor = -2\)
      • \(\lfloor 2 \rfloor = 2\)
      • \(\lfloor 0.2 \rfloor = 0\)
      • \(\lfloor -0.3 \rfloor = -1\)
  2. Ceiling Function \(\lceil x \rceil\):
    • Definition: The ceiling function, also called the least integer function, gives the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to \(x\).
    • Examples:
      • \(\lceil 2.4 \rceil = 3\)
      • \(\lceil 1.9 \rceil = 2\)
      • \(\lceil 0 \rceil = 0\)
      • \(\lceil -1.2 \rceil = -1\)
      • \(\lceil 2 \rceil = 2\)
      • \(\lceil 0.2 \rceil = 1\)
      • \(\lceil -0.3 \rceil = 0\)
4.3. Composition of Functions (Chapter 2, Example)

Let \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) and \(g(x) = x+1\). Find the compositions \((f \circ g)(x)\), \((g \circ f)(x)\), \((f \circ f)(x)\), and \((g \circ g)(x)\) and their respective domains.

Click to see the solution
  1. \((f \circ g)(x)\):
    • \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x+1) = \sqrt{x+1}\).
    • Domain: For the output to be real, we need \(x+1 \ge 0 \implies x \ge -1\). Domain is \([-1, \infty)\).
  2. \((g \circ f)(x)\):
    • \((g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(\sqrt{x}) = \sqrt{x}+1\).
    • Domain: For the input of \(f(x)\) to be valid, we need \(x \ge 0\). Domain is \([0, \infty)\).
  3. \((f \circ f)(x)\):
    • \((f \circ f)(x) = f(f(x)) = f(\sqrt{x}) = \sqrt{\sqrt{x}} = x^{1/4}\).
    • Domain: For the input of the outer \(f\) to be valid, we need \(f(x) \ge 0\), which is always true for \(\sqrt{x}\). For the input of the inner \(f\), we need \(x \ge 0\). Domain is \([0, \infty)\).
  4. \((g \circ g)(x)\):
    • \((g \circ g)(x) = g(g(x)) = g(x+1) = (x+1)+1 = x+2\).
    • Domain: The domain of linear functions is all real numbers. Domain is \((-\infty, \infty)\).
4.4. Prove Inverse Trigonometric Identities (Chapter 2, Proofs)

Prove the following identities for inverse trigonometric functions:

  1. \(\arcsin(x) + \arccos(x) = \frac{\pi}{2}\) for \(x \in [-1, 1]\).
  2. \(\arcsin(-x) = -\arcsin(x)\) for \(x \in [-1, 1]\).
Click to see the solution

(a) \(\arcsin(x) + \arccos(x) = \frac{\pi}{2}\)

  1. Let \(\theta = \arcsin(x)\). By definition, this means \(\sin(\theta) = x\) and \(\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\).
  2. Using the co-function identity, we know that \(\cos(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta) = \sin(\theta)\).
  3. Therefore, \(\cos(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta) = x\).
  4. Since \(\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\), the angle \((\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta)\) is in the interval \([0, \pi]\), which is the range of the arccos function.
  5. From the definition of arccos, it follows that \(\arccos(x) = \frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\).
  6. Substituting back \(\theta = \arcsin(x)\), we get \(\arccos(x) = \frac{\pi}{2} - \arcsin(x)\), which rearranges to the desired identity.

(b) \(\arcsin(-x) = -\arcsin(x)\)

  1. Let \(\theta = \arcsin(x)\). This means \(\sin(\theta) = x\) and \(\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\).
  2. The sine function is an odd function, so \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin(\theta) = -x\).
  3. Since \(\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\), the angle \(-\theta\) is also in the interval \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\).
  4. From the definition of arcsin, it follows that \(\arcsin(-x) = -\theta\).
  5. Substituting back \(\theta = \arcsin(x)\) gives \(\arcsin(-x) = -\arcsin(x)\).
4.5. Prove an Inverse Trigonometric Identity (Chapter 2, Proof)

Prove the following identity: \(\arcsin(\frac{1}{x}) = \text{arccsc}(x)\) for \(x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).

Click to see the solution
  1. Let \(\theta = \arcsin(\frac{1}{x})\). By the definition of the arcsin function, this means \(\sin(\theta) = \frac{1}{x}\).
  2. Use the reciprocal identity. The definition of the cosecant function is \(\csc(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sin(\theta)}\).
  3. Substitute. From step 1, we can substitute \(\frac{1}{x}\) for \(\sin(\theta)\), which gives \(\csc(\theta) = \frac{1}{1/x} = x\).
  4. Apply the inverse cosecant function. The statement \(\csc(\theta) = x\) is, by definition, equivalent to \(\theta = \text{arccsc}(x)\).
  5. Conclusion. We started with \(\theta = \arcsin(\frac{1}{x})\) and have shown that \(\theta = \text{arccsc}(x)\). Therefore, the two expressions must be equal.
4.6. List Logarithmic Forms of Inverse Hyperbolic Functions (Chapter 2, List)

List the logarithmic form for each of the six inverse hyperbolic functions and their respective domains.

Click to see the solution
  1. \(\sinh^{-1} x = \ln (x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1}), \quad -\infty < x < \infty\).
  2. \(\cosh^{-1} x = \ln (x + \sqrt{x^2 - 1}), \quad x \ge 1\).
  3. \(\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right), \quad |x| < 1\).
  4. \(\text{sech}^{-1} x = \ln \left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}\right), \quad 0 < x \le 1\).
  5. \(\text{csch}^{-1} x = \ln \left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|}\right), \quad x \neq 0\).
  6. \(\coth^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right), \quad |x| > 1\).
4.7. Derive the Logarithmic Form of \(\sinh^{-1}(x)\) (Chapter 2, Proof relation 1)

Prove the first formula: \(\sinh^{-1} x = \ln (x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1})\).

Click to see the solution
  1. Let \(y = \sinh^{-1}(x)\). By definition, \(x = \sinh(y)\).
  2. Use the exponential definition of \(\sinh(y)\): \(x = \frac{e^y - e^{-y}}{2}\).
  3. Multiply by 2 and then by \(e^y\) to clear the denominator and negative exponent: \(2x = e^y - e^{-y} \implies 2xe^y = e^{2y} - 1\).
  4. Rearrange into a quadratic equation in terms of \(e^y\): \((e^y)^2 - 2x(e^y) - 1 = 0\).
  5. Let \(z = e^y\). The equation is \(z^2 - 2xz - 1 = 0\). Solve for \(z\) using the quadratic formula:
    • \(z = \frac{-(-2x) \pm \sqrt{(-2x)^2 - 4(1)(-1)}}{2} = \frac{2x \pm \sqrt{4x^2+4}}{2} = x \pm \sqrt{x^2+1}\).
  6. Since \(z=e^y\), it must be positive. The term \(\sqrt{x^2+1}\) is always greater than \(|x|\). Therefore, the root \(x - \sqrt{x^2+1}\) is always negative. We must take the positive root.
    • \(e^y = x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\).
  7. Take the natural logarithm of both sides to solve for \(y\): \(y = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2+1})\).
4.8. Derive the Logarithmic Form of \(\tanh^{-1}(x)\) (Chapter 2, Proof relation 3)

Prove the third formula: \(\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\).

Click to see the solution
  1. Let \(y = \tanh^{-1}(x)\). By definition, \(x = \tanh(y)\).
  2. Use the exponential definition: \(x = \frac{e^y - e^{-y}}{e^y + e^{-y}}\).
  3. Multiply numerator and denominator by \(e^y\): \(x = \frac{e^{2y}-1}{e^{2y}+1}\).
  4. Solve for \(e^{2y}\):
    • \(x(e^{2y}+1) = e^{2y}-1\).
    • \(xe^{2y}+x = e^{2y}-1\).
    • \(x+1 = e^{2y}-xe^{2y} = e^{2y}(1-x)\).
    • \(e^{2y} = \frac{1+x}{1-x}\).
  5. Take the natural logarithm of both sides to solve for \(y\):
    • \(2y = \ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\).
    • \(y = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\).
4.9. Derive the Logarithmic Form of \(\text{csch}^{-1}(x)\) (Chapter 2, Proof 5)

Prove the fifth formula: \(\text{csch}^{-1} x = \ln \left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|}\right)\).

Click to see the solution
  1. Let \(y = \text{csch}^{-1}(x)\). By definition, \(x = \text{csch}(y)\).
  2. Use the exponential definition: \(x = \frac{1}{\sinh y} = \frac{2}{e^y - e^{-y}}\).
  3. Solve for \(e^y\):
    • \(e^y - e^{-y} = \frac{2}{x}\).
    • Multiply by \(e^y\): \(e^{2y} - 1 = \frac{2}{x}e^y\).
    • Rearrange into a quadratic equation: \((e^y)^2 - \frac{2}{x}(e^y) - 1 = 0\).
  4. Let \(z=e^y\). Solve \(z^2 - \frac{2}{x}z - 1 = 0\) using the quadratic formula:
    • \(z = \frac{2/x \pm \sqrt{4/x^2+4}}{2} = \frac{1}{x} \pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{x^2}+1} = \frac{1}{x} \pm \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{x^2} = \frac{1}{x} \pm \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|}\).
  5. Since \(z=e^y\) must be positive, we must choose the correct root. The term \(\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|}\) is always positive. If we take the minus sign, the result could be negative (e.g., if x is positive and small). The plus sign guarantees a positive result.
    • \(e^y = \frac{1}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|}\).
  6. Take the natural logarithm: \(y = \ln(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|})\).
4.10. Domain and Range of Common Functions (Chapter 2, Example)

State the domain and range for the following common functions: \(y=x^2\), \(y=1/x\), \(y=\sqrt{x}\), \(y=\sqrt{4-x}\), \(y=\sqrt{4-x^2}\).

Click to see the solution
  1. \(y = x^2\) (Parabola):
    • Domain: The function is defined for all real numbers. Domain is \((-\infty, \infty)\).
    • Range: The square of any real number is non-negative. Range is \([0, \infty)\).
  2. \(y = 1/x\) (Hyperbola):
    • Domain: The function is defined for all real numbers except where the denominator is zero. Domain is \((-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty)\).
    • Range: The function can take any real value except zero. Range is \((-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty)\).
  3. \(y = \sqrt{x}\) (Square Root):
    • Domain: The expression under the square root must be non-negative. Domain is \([0, \infty)\).
    • Range: The principal square root is always non-negative. Range is \([0, \infty)\).
  4. \(y = \sqrt{4-x}\):
    • Domain: We require \(4-x \ge 0 \implies x \le 4\). Domain is \((-\infty, 4]\).
    • Range: The output is always non-negative. Range is \([0, \infty)\).
  5. \(y = \sqrt{4-x^2}\) (Semicircle):
    • Domain: We require \(4-x^2 \ge 0 \implies x^2 \le 4 \implies -2 \le x \le 2\). Domain is \([-2, 2]\).
    • Range: The minimum value is 0 (at \(x=\pm 2\)) and the maximum value is \(\sqrt{4-0}=2\) (at \(x=0\)). Range is $$.
4.11. Prove a Hyperbolic-Inverse Trig Identity (Chapter 2, Proof 1)

Prove the identity \(\sinh(\text{arccosh}(x)) = \sqrt{x^2-1}\) for \(|x| \ge 1\).

Click to see the solution
  1. Set up the variables: Let \(y = \text{arccosh}(x)\). By the definition of the inverse hyperbolic cosine, this means \(x = \cosh(y)\).
  2. Use the fundamental hyperbolic identity: \(\cosh^2(y) - \sinh^2(y) = 1\).
  3. Solve for \(\sinh(y)\):
    • \(\sinh^2(y) = \cosh^2(y) - 1\).
    • Substitute \(x = \cosh(y)\): \(\sinh^2(y) = x^2 - 1\).
  4. Take the square root:
    • \(\sinh(y) = \pm\sqrt{x^2-1}\).
  5. Determine the sign: The range of the arccosh function is \(y \ge 0\). For non-negative values of \(y\), the function \(\sinh(y)\) is also non-negative. Therefore, we must take the positive root.
    • \(\sinh(y) = \sqrt{x^2-1}\).
  6. Substitute back: Since \(y = \text{arccosh}(x)\), we have \(\sinh(\text{arccosh}(x)) = \sqrt{x^2-1}\).
4.12. Prove an Inequality by Induction (Lab 4, Task 1.1)

Prove the following statement by induction: \(\sin^{2n}(\alpha) + \cos^{2n}(\alpha) \le 1\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

Click to see the solution

Let \(P(n)\) be the statement \(\sin^{2n}(\alpha) + \cos^{2n}(\alpha) \le 1\).

  1. Base Step (n=1):
    • For \(n=1\), the statement is \(\sin^2(\alpha) + \cos^2(\alpha) \le 1\).
    • By the fundamental Pythagorean identity, \(\sin^2(\alpha) + \cos^2(\alpha) = 1\).
    • Since \(1 \le 1\) is true, the base case holds.
  2. Inductive Step:
    • Assumption (Inductive Hypothesis): Assume \(P(k)\) is true for some positive integer \(k\). That is, \(\sin^{2k}(\alpha) + \cos^{2k}(\alpha) \le 1\).
    • Goal: Prove that \(P(k+1)\) is true: \(\sin^{2(k+1)}(\alpha) + \cos^{2(k+1)}(\alpha) \le 1\).
    • Proof:
      • Consider the expression for \(P(k+1)\): \(\sin^{2k+2}(\alpha) + \cos^{2k+2}(\alpha) = \sin^{2k}(\alpha)\sin^2(\alpha) + \cos^{2k}(\alpha)\cos^2(\alpha)\).
      • Since \(0 \le \sin^2(\alpha) \le 1\) and \(0 \le \cos^2(\alpha) \le 1\), we can say:
        • \(\sin^{2k}(\alpha)\sin^2(\alpha) \le \sin^{2k}(\alpha)\).
        • \(\cos^{2k}(\alpha)\cos^2(\alpha) \le \cos^{2k}(\alpha)\).
      • Adding these two inequalities gives: \(\sin^{2k+2}(\alpha) + \cos^{2k+2}(\alpha) \le \sin^{2k}(\alpha) + \cos^{2k}(\alpha)\).
      • By our inductive hypothesis, we know that \(\sin^{2k}(\alpha) + \cos^{2k}(\alpha) \le 1\).
      • Therefore, by transitivity, \(\sin^{2k+2}(\alpha) + \cos^{2k+2}(\alpha) \le 1\). This proves \(P(k+1)\) is true.
  3. Conclusion: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement holds for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
4.13. Prove Divisibility by Induction (Lab 4, Task 1.2)

Show that \(5(2^{3n-2}) + 3^{3n-1}\) is divisible by 19 for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

Click to see the solution

Let \(P(n) = 5(2^{3n-2}) + 3^{3n-1}\).

  1. Base Step (n=1):
    • For \(n=1\), \(P(1) = 5(2^{3(1)-2}) + 3^{3(1)-1} = 5(2^1) + 3^2 = 10 + 9 = 19\).
    • Since \(19\) is divisible by 19, the base case is true.
  2. Inductive Step:
    • Assumption (Inductive Hypothesis): Assume \(P(k)\) is divisible by 19 for some positive integer \(k\). That is, \(5(2^{3k-2}) + 3^{3k-1} = 19m\) for some integer \(m\).
    • Goal: Prove that \(P(k+1) = 5(2^{3(k+1)-2}) + 3^{3(k+1)-1}\) is divisible by 19.
    • Proof:
      • \(P(k+1) = 5(2^{3k+1}) + 3^{3k+2} = 5(2^3 \cdot 2^{3k-2}) + 3^3 \cdot 3^{3k-1}\).
      • \(= 8 \cdot [5(2^{3k-2})] + 27 \cdot [3^{3k-1}]\).
      • From the hypothesis, we can write \(5(2^{3k-2}) = 19m - 3^{3k-1}\). Substitute this into the expression:
      • \(= 8(19m - 3^{3k-1}) + 27 \cdot 3^{3k-1}\)
      • \(= 8 \cdot 19m - 8 \cdot 3^{3k-1} + 27 \cdot 3^{3k-1}\)
      • \(= 8 \cdot 19m + 19 \cdot 3^{3k-1}\)
      • \(= 19(8m + 3^{3k-1})\).
    • Since \(m\) and \(k\) are integers, \((8m + 3^{3k-1})\) is an integer. Thus, \(P(k+1)\) is a multiple of 19.
  3. Conclusion: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
4.14. Find Inverse Functions (Lab 4, Task 3)

Find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and identify the domain and range of \(f^{-1}\) for the following functions:

  1. \(f(x) = x^5\)
  2. \(f(x) = (2x^3 + 1)^{1/5}\)
  3. \(f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}-3}\)
Click to see the solution

The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\).

(a) \(f(x) = x^5\)

  • Inverse: Let \(y=x^5\). Solving for \(x\) gives \(x = y^{1/5}\). So, \(f^{-1}(x) = x^{1/5}\).
  • Domain and Range of \(f\): \(D_f = (-\infty, \infty)\), \(R_f = (-\infty, \infty)\).
  • Domain and Range of \(f^{-1}\): \(D_{f^{-1}} = (-\infty, \infty)\), \(R_{f^{-1}} = (-\infty, \infty)\).

(b) \(f(x) = (2x^3 + 1)^{1/5}\)

  • Inverse: Let \(y=(2x^3 + 1)^{1/5}\). Then \(y^5 = 2x^3+1 \implies y^5-1 = 2x^3 \implies x^3 = \frac{y^5-1}{2} \implies x = \sqrt{\frac{y^5-1}{2}}\). So, \(f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{\frac{x^5-1}{2}}\).
  • Domain and Range of \(f\): \(D_f = (-\infty, \infty)\), \(R_f = (-\infty, \infty)\).
  • Domain and Range of \(f^{-1}\): \(D_{f^{-1}} = (-\infty, \infty)\), \(R_{f^{-1}} = (-\infty, \infty)\).

(c) \(f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}-3}\)

  • Inverse: Let \(y=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}-3}\). Then \(y(\sqrt{x}-3) = \sqrt{x} \implies y\sqrt{x}-3y=\sqrt{x} \implies y\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{x}=3y \implies \sqrt{x}(y-1)=3y \implies \sqrt{x} = \frac{3y}{y-1} \implies x = \left(\frac{3y}{y-1}\right)^2\). So, \(f^{-1}(x) = \left(\frac{3x}{x-1}\right)^2\).
  • Domain and Range of \(f\): Domain requires \(x \ge 0\) and \(\sqrt{x} \neq 3 \implies x \neq 9\). So \(D_f = [0, 9) \cup (9, \infty)\). The range is \((-\infty, 0] \cup (1, \infty)\).
  • Domain and Range of \(f^{-1}\): \(D_{f^{-1}} = (-\infty, 0] \cup (1, \infty)\), \(R_{f^{-1}} = [0, 9) \cup (9, \infty)\).
4.15. Properties of Functions (Lab 4, Task 4)

Given \(f(x) = x^2\), choose suitable domains and codomains to make the function:

  1. Surjective
  2. Injective
  3. Bijective
Click to see the solution

Let the function be defined as \(f: A \to B\), where A is the domain and B is the codomain. The range of \(f(x)=x^2\) is \([0, \infty)\).

(a) Surjective: A function is surjective if its codomain equals its range.

  • We can keep the standard domain \(A = \mathbb{R}\).
  • We must set the codomain \(B\) to be the range, so \(B = [0, \infty)\).
  • Example: \(f: \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty)\) is surjective.

(b) Injective: A function is injective (one-to-one) if it passes the horizontal line test. The function \(f(x)=x^2\) fails this test on \(\mathbb{R}\).

  • We must restrict the domain to a part where the function is strictly increasing or decreasing.
  • We can choose the domain \(A = [0, \infty)\) (or \(A = (-\infty, 0]\)).
  • The codomain B can be \(\mathbb{R}\) or any superset of the range.
  • Example: \(f: [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) is injective.

(c) Bijective: A function is bijective if it is both surjective and injective.

  • We must combine the restrictions from the previous parts.
  • We must restrict the domain to make it injective, e.g., \(A = [0, \infty)\).
  • We must set the codomain to equal the range to make it surjective, e.g., \(B = [0, \infty)\).
  • Example: \(f: [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)\) is bijective. Another example is \(f: (-\infty, 0] \to [0, \infty)\).
4.16. Proof by Induction (Test 1, Task 1a)

Prove by induction the following statement: \(1^3 + 2^3 + 3^3 + \dots + n^3 = \frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}\) for all \(n \ge 1\).

Click to see the solution

Let \(P(n)\) be the statement \(1^3 + 2^3 + \dots + n^3 = \frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}\).

  1. Base Step (n=1):
    • LHS = \(1^3 = 1\).
    • RHS = \(\frac{1^2(1+1)^2}{4} = \frac{1 \cdot 4}{4} = 1\).
    • Since LHS = RHS, the statement \(P(1)\) is true.
  2. Inductive Step:
    • Assumption (Inductive Hypothesis): Assume \(P(k)\) is true for some positive integer \(k\). That is, \(1^3 + \dots + k^3 = \frac{k^2(k+1)^2}{4}\).
    • Goal: Prove that \(P(k+1)\) is true: \(1^3 + \dots + (k+1)^3 = \frac{(k+1)^2(k+2)^2}{4}\).
    • Proof:
      • Start with the left-hand side of the goal: LHS = \((1^3 + \dots + k^3) + (k+1)^3\).
      • Substitute the inductive hypothesis: LHS = \(\frac{k^2(k+1)^2}{4} + (k+1)^3\).
      • Find a common denominator and factor out \((k+1)^2\): \(= \frac{k^2(k+1)^2 + 4(k+1)^3}{4} = \frac{(k+1)^2 [k^2 + 4(k+1)]}{4}\).
      • Simplify the expression in the brackets: \(= \frac{(k+1)^2 [k^2 + 4k + 4]}{4}\).
      • Recognize the perfect square: \(= \frac{(k+1)^2 (k+2)^2}{4}\).
    • This is the right-hand side of the goal. Thus, \(P(k+1)\) is true.
  3. Conclusion: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for all integers \(n \ge 1\).
4.17. Proof by Induction (Divisibility) (Test 1, Task 1b)

Prove by induction that \(4 | (9^n + 3)\) for all \(n \ge 0\) (i.e., 4 is a factor of \(9^n+3\)).

Click to see the solution

Let \(P(n)\) be the statement that \(9^n + 3\) is divisible by 4.

  1. Base Step (n=0):
    • For \(n=0\), we have \(9^0 + 3 = 1 + 3 = 4\).
    • Since 4 is divisible by 4, the statement \(P(0)\) is true.
  2. Inductive Step:
    • Assumption (Inductive Hypothesis): Assume \(P(k)\) is true for some integer \(k \ge 0\). That is, \(9^k + 3\) is divisible by 4, which means we can write \(9^k + 3 = 4m\) for some integer \(m\).
    • Goal: Prove that \(P(k+1)\) is true: \(9^{k+1} + 3\) is divisible by 4.
    • Proof:
      • Consider the expression \(9^{k+1} + 3 = 9 \cdot 9^k + 3\).
      • From the hypothesis, we can express \(9^k\) as \(9^k = 4m - 3\). Substitute this into the expression:
      • \(= 9(4m - 3) + 3\)
      • \(= 36m - 27 + 3\)
      • \(= 36m - 24\)
      • \(= 4(9m - 6)\).
    • Since \(m\) is an integer, \((9m - 6)\) is also an integer. Thus, \(9^{k+1} + 3\) is a multiple of 4. This shows \(P(k+1)\) is true.
  3. Conclusion: By the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for all integers \(n \ge 0\).
4.18. Find min, max, sup, and inf of Sets (Test 1, Task 2)

Let \(A = [1, 5)\) and \(B = (1, 5) \cup \{6, 8\}\). Fill in the blanks (put X if there isn’t an answer):

  1. max(A), min(A), sup(A), inf(A)
  2. max(B), min(B), sup(B), inf(B)
Click to see the solution

(a) For \(A = [1, 5)\)

  • max(A) = X: The maximum is the largest element in the set. Since 5 is not included, there is no largest element.
  • min(A) = 1: The minimum is the smallest element in the set. Since 1 is included, it is the minimum.
  • sup(A) = 5: The supremum is the least upper bound. 5 is an upper bound, and any number smaller than 5 is not.
  • inf(A) = 1: The infimum is the greatest lower bound. It is equal to the minimum when a minimum exists.

(b) For \(B = (1, 5) \cup \{6, 8\}\)

  • max(B) = 8: The largest element in the set is 8.
  • min(B) = X: The minimum would be the smallest element. The set gets arbitrarily close to 1 but does not include 1, so there is no minimum.
  • sup(B) = 8: The supremum is the least upper bound, which is the maximum when a maximum exists.
  • inf(B) = 1: The infimum is the greatest lower bound. The set of lower bounds is \((-\infty, 1]\), and the greatest of these is 1.
4.19. Complex Number Arithmetic (Test 1, Task 3a)

Let \(z_1 = -1 + i\) and \(z_2 = -2 - 4i\). Find the following:

  1. \(2z_1 - 3z_2\)
  2. \(\frac{z_1+z_2}{z_1^2}\)
Click to see the solution

(a) \(2z_1 - 3z_2\)

  1. Substitute the values: \(2(-1 + i) - 3(-2 - 4i)\).
  2. Distribute the scalars: \((-2 + 2i) - (-6 - 12i)\).
  3. Combine real and imaginary parts: \((-2 + 6) + (2i + 12i) = 4 + 14i\).

(b) \(\frac{z_1+z_2}{z_1^2}\)

  1. Calculate the numerator: \(z_1 + z_2 = (-1 + i) + (-2 - 4i) = -3 - 3i\).
  2. Calculate the denominator: \(z_1^2 = (-1 + i)^2 = (-1)^2 + 2(-1)(i) + i^2 = 1 - 2i - 1 = -2i\).
  3. Perform the division: \(\frac{-3 - 3i}{-2i}\).
  4. Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: \(\frac{-3 - 3i}{-2i} \cdot \frac{2i}{2i} = \frac{-6i - 6i^2}{-4i^2}\).
  5. Simplify: \(\frac{-6i - 6(-1)}{-4(-1)} = \frac{6 - 6i}{4} = \frac{6}{4} - \frac{6}{4}i = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{3}{2}i\).

Answer:

  1. \(4 + 14i\)
  2. \(\frac{3}{2} - \frac{3}{2}i\)
4.20. Trigonometric and Exponential Forms of a Complex Number (Test 1, Task 3b)

Find the trigonometric and exponential forms of \(z_1 = -1 + i\).

Click to see the solution
  1. Find the Modulus (r): The modulus is the distance from the origin to the point \((-1, 1)\) in the complex plane.
    • \(r = |z_1| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{1+1} = \sqrt{2}\).
  2. Find the Argument (\(\theta\)): The argument is the angle the vector makes with the positive real axis.
    • The point \((-1, 1)\) is in the second quadrant.
    • The reference angle is \(\arctan\left(\frac{|1|}{|-1|}\right) = \arctan(1) = \pi/4\).
    • In the second quadrant, the angle is \(\theta = \pi - (\text{reference angle}) = \pi - \pi/4 = 3\pi/4\).
  3. Write the Trigonometric Form: The form is \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\).
    • \(z_1 = \sqrt{2}\left(\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\right)\).
  4. Write the Exponential Form: The form is \(z = re^{i\theta}\).
    • \(z_1 = \sqrt{2}e^{i3\pi/4}\).

Answer:

  • Trigonometric: \(\sqrt{2}(\cos(3\pi/4) + i\sin(3\pi/4))\)
  • Exponential: \(\sqrt{2}e^{i3\pi/4}\)
4.21. Prove a Function is One-to-One and Find its Inverse (Test 1, Task 4)

Let \(f(x) = \frac{x-2}{2x-3}\). Does \(f\) represent a one-to-one function (prove)? If Yes, Find \(f^{-1}\).

Click to see the solution

Part 1: Prove the function is one-to-one

  1. Definition of one-to-one: A function \(f\) is one-to-one if for any \(a, b\) in the domain of \(f\), the condition \(f(a)=f(b)\) implies that \(a=b\).
  2. Set up the equation: Assume \(f(a) = f(b)\) for some \(a\) and \(b\) in the domain.
    • \(\frac{a-2}{2a-3} = \frac{b-2}{2b-3}\).
  3. Solve for \(a\):
    • Cross-multiply: \((a-2)(2b-3) = (b-2)(2a-3)\).
    • Expand both sides: \(2ab - 3a - 4b + 6 = 2ab - 3b - 4a + 6\).
    • Subtract \(2ab\) and 6 from both sides: \(-3a - 4b = -3b - 4a\).
    • Add \(4a\) and \(4b\) to both sides: \(a = b\).
  4. Conclusion: Since \(f(a)=f(b)\) implies \(a=b\), the function is one-to-one.

Part 2: Find the inverse function \(f^{-1}\)

  1. Replace \(f(x)\) with y: \(y = \frac{x-2}{2x-3}\).
  2. Solve for x in terms of y:
    • \(y(2x-3) = x-2\).
    • \(2xy - 3y = x-2\).
    • \(2xy - x = 3y - 2\).
    • Factor out x: \(x(2y-1) = 3y-2\).
    • \(x = \frac{3y-2}{2y-1}\).
  3. Swap x and y to get the inverse function:
    • \(y = \frac{3x-2}{2x-1}\).
Answer: Yes, the function is one-to-one. The inverse is \(f^{-1}(x) = \frac{3x-2}{2x-1}\).
